phil:mackie: J.L. Mackie was an Australian philosopher best known for his defense of moral skepticism and his contributions to metaethics, philosophy of religion, and the theory of causation. In his 1977 book Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong, he advanced the "error theory," arguing that ordinary moral judgments presuppose objective values that do not in fact exist, so all such claims are systematically false. He is also remembered for a sharp formulation of the logical problem of evil and for influential work on Locke and Hume.
phil:williams: Bernard Williams was an English moral philosopher whose work challenged the ambitions of systematic ethical theory, especially utilitarianism and Kantianism. He argued that impartial moral systems neglect the personal projects, commitments, and character that give an individual's life meaning, introducing influential ideas such as "moral luck" and the notion that theories can demand "one thought too many." His books, including Ethics and the Limits of Philosophy, pressed philosophers to take seriously the complexity and integrity of the individual moral agent.
phil:frankfurt: Harry Frankfurt was an American philosopher known for his work on free will, moral responsibility, and the nature of personhood. He argued that what matters for freedom and responsibility is not the ability to do otherwise but the structure of one's desires, distinguishing first-order desires from the "second-order" desires by which we endorse or reject them, and he devised the influential "Frankfurt cases" that question whether alternate possibilities are required for responsibility. He also reached a wide audience with his essay On Bullshit, an analysis of speech indifferent to truth.
phil:korsgaard: Christine Korsgaard is an American philosopher and a leading contemporary interpreter and defender of Kantian ethics. Her work argues that moral obligations arise from the reflective nature of human agency: because we can step back from our impulses and ask whether to act on them, we must confer value on ourselves and, in turn, on others, a view she develops in The Sources of Normativity. She has also written extensively on personal identity, practical reason, and the moral standing of animals.
phil:gilligan: Carol Gilligan is an American psychologist and ethicist whose research reshaped debates about moral development and gender. In her 1982 book In a Different Voice, she criticized prevailing models that treated abstract justice reasoning as the highest stage of moral maturity, arguing that they overlooked an equally valid "ethic of care" attentive to relationships, responsibility, and context. Her work became foundational for care ethics and for feminist philosophy more broadly.
phil:noddings: Nel Noddings was an American philosopher of education and a principal architect of the ethics of care. She argued that morality is grounded not in abstract principles but in the concrete relation between a "one-caring" and a "cared-for," developing this view most fully in her 1984 book Caring. Her work applied the ethics of care to teaching and schooling, emphasizing responsiveness, attentiveness, and the moral significance of human relationships.
phil:macintyre: Alasdair MacIntyre is a Scottish-born philosopher whose work mounted an influential critique of modern moral philosophy and a revival of virtue ethics. In After Virtue (1981) he argued that Enlightenment attempts to justify morality on rational grounds had failed, leaving moral discourse fragmented, and he called for a return to an Aristotelian and Thomistic tradition in which the virtues are understood within practices, narrative lives, and communities. His thought has been central to debates about tradition, rationality, and community in ethics.
phil:nussbaum: Martha Nussbaum is an American philosopher who works across ethics, political philosophy, ancient thought, and law. With economist Amartya Sen she helped develop the "capabilities approach," which measures human well-being and justice by what people are actually able to do and to be rather than by wealth or preference satisfaction. She is also known for defending the role of emotions in ethical reasoning and for wide-ranging writing on literature, education, and human dignity.
phil:anscombe: Elizabeth Anscombe was a British analytic philosopher and a student of Ludwig Wittgenstein, whose translations and editing helped bring his later work to an English-speaking audience. Her 1957 monograph Intention founded modern philosophy of action, analyzing intentional action in terms of a distinctive kind of knowledge and reasons for acting. Her 1958 essay "Modern Moral Philosophy" attacked rule-based ethics detached from a theory of human flourishing and is widely credited with reviving virtue ethics and coining the term "consequentialism."
phil:adam-smith: Adam Smith was a Scottish philosopher and economist central to the Enlightenment, best remembered as the founder of modern economics through The Wealth of Nations (1776). Yet he was first a moral philosopher, and in The Theory of Moral Sentiments he argued that moral judgment rests on sympathy and on the imagined perspective of an "impartial spectator." His work links human sociability, self-interest, and the workings of markets within a broad account of moral and social life.
phil:wolf: Susan Wolf is an American moral philosopher known for questioning whether being perfectly moral is a coherent or desirable ideal. In her essay "Moral Saints" she argued that a life devoted wholly to morality would be strangely impoverished, lacking the personal passions and pursuits that make a life good. She has also written influentially on free will and moral responsibility and on the sources of meaning in life, contending that meaning arises when subjective engagement meets objective worth.
phil:hobbes: Thomas Hobbes was an English philosopher and a founder of modern political thought, writing during the upheavals of the English Civil War. In Leviathan (1651) he argued that in a "state of nature" without government human life would be a war of all against all—"solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short"—and that rational individuals would therefore contract to submit to a powerful sovereign in exchange for security. His materialist account of human beings and his social-contract justification of political authority shaped centuries of debate.
phil:rousseau: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was a Genevan-born philosopher of the Enlightenment whose work profoundly influenced political thought, education, and Romanticism. In The Social Contract (1762) he argued that legitimate authority rests on the "general will" of a self-governing people, famously opening with the claim that "man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains." He held that civilization had corrupted a naturally good humanity, a theme also developed in his writings on inequality and on education in Émile.
phil:machiavelli: Niccolò Machiavelli was a Florentine diplomat, historian, and political theorist of the Renaissance, often called a founder of modern political science. His notorious treatise The Prince (written 1513) analyzed how rulers actually gain and keep power, arguing that a leader must be willing to act against conventional morality when necessity demands, judging conduct by results rather than intentions. His broader Discourses on Livy reveal a committed republican, and his realism about politics gave rise to the term "Machiavellian."
phil:rawls: John Rawls was an American political philosopher whose A Theory of Justice (1971) revived and reshaped liberal political philosophy in the twentieth century. He argued that principles of justice are those that free and equal persons would choose from an "original position" behind a "veil of ignorance" that hides their own social place, yielding a scheme that protects equal basic liberties and permits inequalities only when they benefit the least advantaged. His later work, Political Liberalism, addressed how a just society can endure amid deep disagreement about values.
